newsitem.title: USA: U.N. ambassador says U.S. must pay debt.
newsitem.headline: U.N. ambassador says U.S. must pay debt.

text.p: Ambassador to the United Nations Bill Richardson told Congress on Wednesday that America must pay its U.N. debt to maintain its influence and win reforms that would reduce its future dues.
"We are losing our influence and our leverage there," Richardson told a House of Represenatives appropriations subcommittee.
Unless the United States pays its U.N. arrears of more than $1 billion, he said, "We are not going to achieve reforms for others to pay more so we can pay less."
He said the United States wants reforms that will reduce its peacekeeping assessment to 25 percent of the total from 30.8 percent, and its annual U.N. dues to 20 percent of the total from 25 percent.
But Richardson said in his first testimony to Congress after a month in his new job that other U.N. members were deeply resentful of the unpaid U.S. debt.

"As I advance a proposal I see the 14 other member states of the Security Council basically almost whispering under their breath 'So you want us to do this? Why don't you pay your bills?' That is a reduction in influence," he said.
Richardson said the U.N. calculates the U.S. debt at $1.6 billion, but Washington says the debt is just over $1 billion because of disputes over what should be included.
Richardson praised U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan's announcement of reforms on Monday including elimination of 1,000 U.N. jobs and a $123 million budget cut.
However, the U.S. ambassador said the Clinton administration will announce its own reform proposals in the next day or so going further.

Members of the congressional subcommittee agreed the United States should pay its debt, one of them readily suggesting the United States has been "a piker" on the debt, but they disagreed on when it should pay in order to assure that the U.N. approves reforms Washington wants.

Clinton has asked Congress to approve part of the arrearage payment quickly, though the United Nations would not get the money until reforms are approved. But Representative Harold Rogers, a Kentucky Republican and chairman of the subcommittee, bluntly told Richardson "that's not going to happen."
Rogers also said he was sceptical of Annan's reforms because the 1,000 jobs, for example, are already vacant. Richardson praised Annan for eliminating them so they cannot be refilled.
